threats.name: Broken object-level authorization on score, exam-result and export reads
threats.description: Every read path that takes a member identifier — score detail, exam result, self export, ranked list, chart dataset — must re-derive entitlement from the caller's authorization context rather than honour the identifier in the request. This is the classic failure mode of exactly this kind of API and the specification carries no per-endpoint enforcement design.
threats.attackScenario: An authenticated Team Member observes the request their own dashboard makes, substitutes a colleague's member identifier, and receives that colleague's full per-skill score history and exam results. Repeating across the identifier space yields the entire organization's assessment dataset.
threats.businessImpact: Mass exposure of employment-relevant performance data about every identifiable individual in the organization. Loss of trust in the assessment programme, likely personal-data breach notification depending on SQ-1.
mitigations: Resolve object entitlement inside the owning component from the server-side authorization context, never from a request-supplied identifier (SEC-AUTHZ-2).

Build the authorization matrix (4 roles x every entry point x operation) as an executable test fixture before the first endpoint is written; REQUIREMENT_TEMPLATE.md already demands authorization test cases per requirement.
Make the deny case the default in the framework layer so a new endpoint is unreachable until a rule permits it.
Use unguessable identifiers as defence in depth only — never as the access control.

threats.name: Privilege escalation to Administrator
owasp: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
threats.description: Three distinct routes converge on the same outcome: mass assignment of a role field on a profile update; direct invocation of an account or role endpoint by a non-Administrator; and — if SQ-10 resolves the wrong way — a role or group claim asserted by the OIDC provider and accepted as authoritative. FR-1.3 makes role assignment Administrator-only, but no mechanism enforces that across all three routes.
threats.attackScenario: A Team Member updates their own profile, appending a role field set to Administrator. The handler binds the request body to the user model wholesale. The next request carries Administrator authority: full access to every score, every answer key, the audit trail, and the deletion capability.
threats.businessImpact: Total compromise of the assessment dataset and its integrity, including undetectable-by-design score manipulation if the attacker also controls the audit trail's retention.
mitigations: Bind request bodies to explicit allow-listed field sets per endpoint; never bind wholesale to a persistence model (SEC-INPUT-3).
Make role a field only the account-administration endpoint can write, and forbid self-role modification outright even for an Administrator.

Answer SQ-10 and record the decision: role is assigned locally by an Administrator (FR-1.3) and any OIDC role or group claim is ignored. If the provider must be trusted for role, that is a separate accepted risk with its own compensating controls.
Include self-role-modification and mass-assignment cases in the standing authorization test suite.

threats.name: Exam answer-key disclosure through an over-returned exam payload
owasp: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
threats.description: NFR-9.7 forbids answer keys reaching a Team Member or Viewer at any point. The realistic failure is not a deliberate leak but an exam object serialized whole — the questions carry their correct answers as a field, the client hides them, and the network payload contains them. Error paths, cached responses, debug output and source maps are the same hazard.
threats.attackScenario: A Team Member opens an assigned exam and inspects the network response, which contains each question with its correctAnswer field because the model was serialized whole and the client filters for display. The answers are shared; every exam-derived score in the organization becomes meaningless.
threats.businessImpact: Silent, permanent destruction of the integrity of the entire assessment programme — the product's core value. Damage is not detectable from within the system: scores look normal.
mitigations: Model the exam-attempt payload as a distinct type that has no answer-key field to omit — structural exclusion beats filtering.
Exclude inside Assessment before the response is assembled, never in a serializer, view layer or client (SEC-BOUND-3).

Add a standing test asserting no answer-key field appears in any Team Member or Viewer response, including error and debug paths, and run it against the recorded network payload, not the handler's return value.
Never include answer keys in a chart, export, audit or log record (SEC-LOG-3).

threats.name: Peer score exposure through the shared radar chart
threats.description: A specification contradiction, not an implementation bug. FR-1.4 forbids a Team Member seeing another individual's scores except within a shared-team radar chart; FR-7.3 requires each series be attributed to its member by name; FR-6.2 requires the same dataset be available as a table; DR-7 requires both come from one payload. The exception therefore delivers exactly what the rule withholds, in machine-readable form. SEC-AUTHZ-3 describes the chart series as aggregated, which it is not.
threats.attackScenario: No attack is required. A Team Member opens the chart for a team they belong to and reads every colleague's exact per-skill score from the accompanying table, or from the JSON payload. If team membership is broad, this is the whole organization.
threats.businessImpact: Peer-visible performance ranking with no policy decision behind it. In an employment context this carries morale, grievance and — subject to SQ-1 — regulatory consequences. The organization cannot state its own confidentiality posture because the specification does not have one.

existingControls.status: Specified — Not Implemented; and ambiguous as written

mitigations: Answer OQ-1 explicitly and record the decision in REQUIREMENTS.md as the owning document. The three plausible answers are: peers see attributed scores (status quo by default), peers see only their own series plus an unattributed team envelope or median, or shared charts are visible only to Assessor, Administrator and Viewer roles.

Whichever is chosen, make the Chart Data Service enforce it server-side — the dataset must not contain a value the caller may not see, because DR-7 guarantees the table shows whatever the chart receives (SEC-DATA-4).
Amend SEC-AUTHZ-3 to stop describing the series as aggregated, or make it actually aggregated.
threats.note: Not self-identified by the specification corpus. One of the two contradictions this engagement adds.

threats.name: JWT verification bypass through algorithm or claim confusion
threats.description: JWT is chosen as the session mechanism but the algorithm, key handling and token-type split are all TO BE DECIDED. The standard failures follow: accepting alg none, accepting a caller-chosen algorithm, confusing an asymmetric public key for an HMAC secret, or verifying the signature without verifying issuer, audience and expiry.
threats.attackScenario: An attacker presents a token with the algorithm header set to none, or signs one with the published verification key treated as an HMAC secret, and receives whatever role the payload claims.
threats.businessImpact: Complete authentication bypass; equivalent to T-02 in outcome.
mitigations: Pin one signing algorithm server-side and reject any token whose header differs; never read the algorithm from the token to decide how to verify it.
Verify signature, issuer, audience and expiry on every request (SEC-SESSION-1).
Keep the signing key in the secret store, rotatable without redeploy, with an overlap window for tokens issued moments before rotation (SEC-SECRET-2).
Write the negative tests SEC-SESSION-1 already names — none, wrong algorithm, wrong issuer, wrong audience, expired, tampered payload — as part of the first authentication PR.

threats.name: Stale authority: revoked or role-changed sessions keep working
threats.description: Self-contained JWTs carry authority that outlives the decision that granted it. FR-1.3 lets an Administrator deactivate an account or change a role; SEC-SESSION-3 requires that to take effect without waiting for token expiry, but the revocation mechanism, token lifetimes and refresh model are all TO BE DECIDED (SQ-5). SEC-SESSION-2 additionally requires that authorization-relevant claims be re-resolved server-side rather than trusted from the token.
threats.attackScenario: An employee is deactivated during an offboarding. Their existing access token remains valid for its lifetime, and every request it makes is authorized from claims baked in before the deactivation. If the token also carries the role claim, a demoted Assessor keeps writing scores.
threats.businessImpact: Offboarding and demotion do not take effect when the business believes they do — the gap between intent and enforcement is exactly the window an aggrieved departing employee occupies.
mitigations: Answer SQ-5 with a short access-token lifetime plus a revocable refresh token, or server-side session state consulted per request.
Re-resolve role, assessor team assignments and member correspondence from Identity & Access and Roster at authorization time; treat the token as identity only (SEC-SESSION-2).
Issue a new session identifier on authentication and on any privilege change, invalidating the prior one (SEC-SESSION-5).
Test that deactivation blocks the very next protected request on an already-issued token.

threats.name: Exam result forgery through client-supplied score
owasp: API6:2023 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
threats.description: FR-5.7 derives a 1-10 score from the percentage of correct answers. If the submission handler accepts a score, percentage or correct-count field from the client, or trusts a client-side computation, the member sets their own result. SEC-BIZ-1 and SEC-INPUT-3 forbid it; nothing yet enforces it.
threats.attackScenario: A Team Member submits an exam with an added score field of 10, or edits the client bundle to post a precomputed percentage. The recorded score, its method stamp of exam-derived, and its appearance on every chart all say the member scored top marks.
threats.businessImpact: Assessment integrity loss that is worse than an answer-key leak because it leaves the same trace as a legitimate result and requires no collusion.
mitigations: Accept only answer selections from the client; compute percentage and band server-side from the stored answer key (SEC-BIZ-1).
Reject or ignore every server-derived field if present in a request: score, method, source, recorded date, audit fields (SEC-INPUT-3).
Test with a forged score field asserting the recorded value derives from the answers only — SEC-BIZ-1 already names this test.

threats.name: Assessor writes scores outside assigned teams, especially through bulk paths
threats.description: FR-1.5 scopes an Assessor to their assigned teams. SEC-AUTHZ-4 extends that to every code path including bulk operations. Bulk and import paths are where per-object authorization is habitually skipped, because the check sits on the request rather than on each row.
threats.attackScenario: An Assessor uploads an import file, or posts a batch score payload, containing member identifiers from teams they are not assigned to. The handler authorizes the operation once, then applies every row.
threats.businessImpact: Score manipulation across organizational boundaries, influencing staffing and promotion decisions outside the actor's remit, with an audit trail that looks like routine bulk work.
mitigations: Authorize per row and per target object, not per request; the import path must call the same server-side rules as interactive entry (SEC-INPUT-4).
Reject the whole import rather than partially applying it when any row fails authorization, consistent with SEC-ERR-2.
Answer SQ-9 on whether bulk import runs as background work — if it does, it needs its own authorization context and audit trail rather than inheriting an ambient one.
Test single and bulk paths with out-of-team identifiers, as SEC-AUTHZ-4 already specifies.

threats.name: Asset reference treated as entitlement for exam media
threats.description: DR-9 and SEC-BOUND-4 state that possession of a reference is not entitlement, but the access-grant mechanism is TO BE DECIDED, so the rule cannot yet be tested. The common shortcut — a long-lived signed URL, or a publicly readable bucket with unguessable keys — silently converts a reference into an entitlement and moves the access decision outside the API.
threats.attackScenario: Exam media URLs are shared, cached by an intermediary, or enumerated. Anyone holding a URL retrieves exam content indefinitely, including after the member's attempt window closes and including unauthenticated parties.
threats.businessImpact: Exam content leak with the same consequence as T-03: exam-derived scores stop meaning anything.
mitigations: Decide the grant mechanism as part of SQ-8 and make each grant single-asset, short-lived and bound to the authorized actor.
Never make the asset store directly reachable from the internet (SEC-CICD-3).
Test that a reference obtained legitimately fails for an unentitled actor and after grant expiry, as SEC-BOUND-4 already specifies.
If exams carry no media, delete the Protected Asset Store from the architecture and close this threat — the requirement to keep it is an ASSUMPTION.

threats.name: Account recovery and emailed link weaknesses become a parallel authentication route
threats.description: Passkeys are strong; the recovery path around them usually is not, and SQ-7 records that the path is undefined. Separately, exam-invitation and account-access links are the only credential-bearing artifacts leaving the system by email, and SEC-AUTHN-8's requirements — single-use, time-bounded, unguessable, recipient-bound, not session-conferring — have no chosen lifetime.
threats.attackScenario: A user loses their passkey. The recovery flow emails a link that establishes a full session. An attacker with mailbox access, or with a predictable token, obtains a session without ever touching the passkey — the strong authenticator is decoration.
threats.businessImpact: Account takeover at the strength of the weakest route, not the advertised one. For an Administrator account, equivalent to T-02.
mitigations: Answer SQ-7: define the recovery path and hold it to the same assurance as the primary one — re-enrolment verified by an Administrator rather than by an emailed link alone for privileged roles.
Generate link tokens from a cryptographic random source, store only their hash, bind them to the recipient account, expire them in minutes not days, and invalidate on first use (SEC-AUTHN-8).
An exam-invitation link must authorize opening that exam, not establish a general session.
Decide whether password authentication is a permanent peer of passkeys or a migration path (SQ-7); a permanent peer means the password path sets the system's true authentication strength.

threats.name: SQL injection through sort, filter and pagination parameters
threats.description: FR-6.3 requires ordering team members by their score for a chosen skill. Sort and filter parameters are the one place parameterization habitually fails, because a column name cannot be bound as a value and gets concatenated instead. SEC-INPUT-6 anticipates exactly this and requires a server-side allow-list.
threats.attackScenario: An authenticated user supplies a crafted sort parameter that is concatenated into the ORDER BY clause, extracting arbitrary rows including credential hashes and answer keys through error or timing channels.
threats.businessImpact: Full database disclosure or modification from any authenticated account — the worst single outcome available in this system.
mitigations: Parameterize every value; map sortable and filterable fields through a server-side allow-list to fixed column expressions, never interpolating the caller's string (SEC-INPUT-6).
Give each domain component a database identity limited to the tables it owns (DR-4), so injection in one component cannot read another's.
Include injection payloads in sort and filter parameters in the standing test suite.

threats.name: Stored XSS through member, team, skill and question text, including chart labels
threats.description: Every displayed name in this system is user-supplied and crosses from one user to another: member names, team names, skill names, exam question text, import error messages, and chart axis and legend labels. React escapes by default, but the radar chart is the exception — chart labels are frequently rendered into SVG or canvas by a library, outside React's escaping, and the library is TO BE DECIDED. Combined with a session token in web storage (SEC-SESSION-4 forbids it, but the transport is undecided), any XSS becomes account takeover.
threats.attackScenario: An Assessor names a skill with a script payload. Every user who loads a chart containing that axis executes it. If the session token is reachable from script, the attacker collects sessions including an Administrator's.
threats.businessImpact: Account takeover chained from an ordinary data-entry field, escalating to T-02 when an Administrator views the chart.
mitigations: Choose the chart library under DEP-1..DEP-8 with this threat as an explicit selection criterion, and verify how it renders text nodes before adopting it.
Render chart labels as text nodes from structured values; never interpolate a server string into SVG, style or canvas markup (SEC-RENDER-2).
Lint-ban raw-HTML injection props and test every displayed name field with markup payloads (SEC-RENDER-1).
Keep the session token out of any script-readable store and decide the CSP directives SEC-HTTP-7 defers.
Validate URL schemes against an allow-list wherever server data becomes a link or deep link (SEC-RENDER-3).

threats.name: Terraform provisions a publicly reachable data store or asset store
threats.description: The single most common cause of mass data exposure in cloud systems is an unintentionally public storage resource. SEC-CICD-3 forbids it unless explicitly intended and documented, and requires IaC scanning in CI — but no cloud provider, no CI system and no Terraform code exist yet (SQ-8), so neither the rule nor the scanner has anything to act on.
threats.attackScenario: The first infrastructure PR creates an object store for exam media with default or over-broad access, or a database reachable from the internet. Nothing in the repository detects it, because run-tests.sh is a placeholder and no IaC scanner is configured.
threats.businessImpact: Unauthenticated exposure of the entire personal performance dataset and exam content, bypassing every application control in this model.

existingControls.status: Specified — Not Implemented; no CI exists

mitigations: Configure an IaC scanner in CI in the same PR that introduces the first .tf file, not after — SEC-CICD-6 requires security checks to block merge.
Default every data resource to private with explicit deny, and require a documented exception for any publicly reachable resource (SEC-CICD-3).
Enable encryption at rest and in transit as a Terraform-level assertion, satisfying SEC-DATA-1 by construction.
Answer SQ-8 before the first infrastructure PR so provider-specific controls can be specified rather than improvised.

threats.name: Self-assessment inflates a member's own displayed score
threats.description: A specification contradiction rather than a coding error. FR-5.2 permits self-assessment, FR-4.6 makes the most recent score current, and FR-5.10 propagates the current score to charts. FR-5.11 requires only that the method be distinguishable in the score detail view — not on the chart. Read literally, a Team Member may set their own charted skill level to 10 at will, and the chart gives the reader no signal.
threats.attackScenario: Before a staffing review, a Team Member self-assesses every skill at 10. The radar chart shows a fully capable engineer. Anyone reading the chart, rather than drilling into each score's detail view, is misled.
threats.businessImpact: The product's headline artifact — the shared radar chart — can be authored by its own subject. Staffing decisions made from it are unsound, and the system gives no warning.

existingControls.status: Specified — covers the detail view only

mitigations: Answer OQ-3 and record it in REQUIREMENTS.md. The defensible options are: self-assessed scores never become the current score, they become current only until superseded by an assessor or exam score, or they are charted as a visually distinct series.
Whatever is chosen, carry the method through to the chart dataset so the client can encode it — and encode it by a means other than color, per NFR-9.4.
Rate-limit and audit self-assessment writes like any other score mutation (SEC-LOG-1).
threats.note: Not self-identified as a security issue by the corpus. The second contradiction this engagement adds.

threats.name: Exam collusion, retake abuse and undefined attempt validity
threats.description: SECURITY.md states it directly: answer-key confidentiality does not by itself prevent collusion. No proctoring, timing, attempt-window or retake policy exists, ARCHITECTURE.md lists attempt timing and resumption as UNKNOWN, and SEC-AUTHZ-8 therefore cannot fully define what a valid attempt is — it can only reject an unassigned, withdrawn or already-completed one.
threats.attackScenario: A member opens an assigned exam, records the questions, consults colleagues, and submits later. Or, with no retake bound, resubmits until the band improves. Neither is distinguishable from legitimate use.
threats.businessImpact: Exam-derived scores drift upward and stop discriminating, undermining the ranking the product exists to produce.
mitigations: Answer SQ-11 with an explicit exam integrity policy: attempt window, time limit, resumption behaviour, retake allowance and cooldown.
Reject submissions outside the attempt window and after completion; record attempt start server-side, never from the client.
Consider question pools or per-attempt ordering so a recorded attempt has limited reuse value.

Accept and document the residual: an unproctored remote exam cannot be made collusion-proof. State that limitation where scores are presented, rather than implying an assurance the method does not provide.

threats.name: Cross-site request forgery on state-changing endpoints
threats.description: SEC-HTTP-3 is CONDITIONAL: CSRF defenses apply only if the web session is an ambient credential. SEC-SESSION-4 forbids localStorage and sessionStorage, which pushes toward a cookie — which makes the condition true. The corpus never closes this loop (SQ-5), so the project can arrive at a cookie session with the CSRF rule still marked conditional and unimplemented.
threats.attackScenario: An authenticated Administrator visits an attacker page, which posts a role change or a score mutation to the API. The browser attaches the session cookie automatically and the request succeeds.
threats.businessImpact: Unauthorized state change under a privileged user's authority, with an audit entry naming that innocent user — which also compromises the NFR-9.6 audit trail's evidential value.
mitigations: Answer SQ-5 and, in the same decision, resolve SEC-HTTP-3 from conditional to required or not-applicable — leaving it conditional past implementation is the actual risk.
If cookies: SameSite plus a per-request anti-forgery token on every state-changing request, and an explicit CORS allow-list with no wildcard alongside credentials (SEC-HTTP-4).
If bearer tokens: keep them out of any script-readable store and accept the XSS coupling described in T-12.

threats.name: Credential stuffing and password brute force
threats.description: The password path is the weakest authenticator the system accepts, and SEC-AUTHN-7's thresholds, windows and lockout behaviour are TO BE DECIDED. Whether password authentication is a permanent peer of passkeys is itself undecided (SQ-7).
threats.attackScenario: An attacker replays a credential dump against the sign-in endpoint. Without per-account throttling, a small fraction succeeds — as it always does.
threats.businessImpact: Account takeover at the rate of password reuse in the organization; disproportionate if a privileged account is hit.
mitigations: Throttle keyed on at least the account identifier, with a rejected attempt indistinguishable from a throttled one (SEC-AUTHN-7).
Store passwords only as a memory-hard salted hash (SEC-AUTHN-4); decide the algorithm and parameters as part of SQ-7.
Require MFA alongside the password path, or make passkeys mandatory for Administrator and Assessor roles — SQ-3 should set assurance per role rather than uniformly.
Check new and changed passwords against a breached-credential list.

threats.name: Account enumeration through authentication and invitation responses
threats.description: SEC-AUTHN-6 requires uniform responses across existing and non-existing identifiers, and SEC-AUTHZ-7 requires the same for denials of records the actor may not see. Timing is the usual leak that survives careful response-body work — and a passkey flow leaks differently from a password flow for the same account.
threats.attackScenario: An attacker probes the sign-in and account-access endpoints with candidate corporate email addresses and learns which are enrolled, building a target list and confirming organizational membership.
threats.businessImpact: Discloses employment relationships and seeds the credential attacks in T-17. Modest alone, useful as a first step.
mitigations: Return one response shape, status code and latency profile for existing and non-existing identifiers on every authentication and recovery endpoint.
Apply the same to authorization denials for object identifiers that do and do not exist (SEC-AUTHZ-7).
Compare timing as well as bodies in the test SEC-AUTHN-6 already specifies.

threats.name: Resource exhaustion through chart datasets, ranked lists and bulk import
threats.description: NFR-9.3 sets 1,000 members and 100 skills, and NFR-9.1 sets a 2-second p95 chart render, while ARCHITECTURE.md records that no read model, index or caching decision has been made. SEC-HTTP-5 and SEC-HTTP-6 require limits whose values are TO BE DECIDED (SQ-9). A chart request is a cross-product query and is the natural amplification primitive here.
threats.attackScenario: An authenticated user repeatedly requests maximum-size chart datasets and deep ranked lists with full score history, or uploads a very large import file, saturating the database and breaching NFR-9.1 for everyone.
threats.businessImpact: Availability loss for a system whose entire value is delivered through the chart, achievable from any ordinary account.
mitigations: Answer SQ-9 with concrete request-rate and request-size limits per endpoint class, and refuse rather than degrade when exceeded (SEC-HTTP-5).
Enforce the FR-7.6 and FR-7.7 chart limits server-side with a stated reason, never by silent truncation (SEC-HTTP-6).
Bound history records returned per request and paginate ranked lists from a server-side allow-list of sort fields (shared with T-11).
Run bulk import as bounded background work with its own limits if SQ-9 resolves that way.
Decide the read model or index strategy ARCHITECTURE.md defers, since NFR-9.1 at NFR-9.3 scale is also an availability control.

threats.name: Concurrent score writes break the one-current-score invariant
threats.description: FR-4.1 permits at most one current score per member per skill and FR-4.6 requires the superseded score to survive as history. SEC-BIZ-2 requires the invariant be enforced in the data store as well as in application logic. Supersede-then-insert is a read-modify-write, and two concurrent writes — an exam submission landing while an assessor rates the same skill — will interleave.
threats.attackScenario: A member submits an exam at the moment an assessor records a rating for the same skill. The system ends with two current scores, or with history missing an entry. A member wanting a specific outcome can deliberately race the two.
threats.businessImpact: The chart shows a non-deterministic value and the audit history has a hole — both fatal to the evidential value of an assessment record used in employment decisions.
mitigations: Enforce one-current-score with a database constraint, such as a partial unique index on (member, skill) where current, so application bugs cannot violate it (SEC-BIZ-2).
Perform supersede and insert in one transaction at an isolation level that prevents the interleaving, or via an append-only history table with the current score derived.
Write the concurrent-write test SEC-BIZ-2 already names, asserting no duplicate current score and no lost history.

threats.name: Partial writes leave a score without its audit entry
threats.description: SEC-ERR-2 names the failure exactly: a score recorded without history, an import half-applied, an exam scored without an audit entry. NFR-9.6 requires an audit entry for every score mutation, which only holds if the entry is part of the same atomic unit as the mutation.
threats.attackScenario: A failure is induced mid-write — or simply occurs — after the score is committed and before the audit entry is. The score exists with no record of who created it. Repeated deliberately, it is a way to change scores without attribution.
threats.businessImpact: The audit trail silently stops being complete, which is worse than having none, because it is relied upon.
mitigations: Write the score, its history record and its audit entry in one transaction; if the audit write cannot succeed, the score write must not either.
Reject a whole import rather than applying it partially (shared with T-08).
Run the failure-injection test SEC-ERR-2 specifies, asserting no partial state.
Add a periodic reconciliation asserting every score mutation has a matching audit entry, so a gap is detected rather than assumed absent.

threats.name: Audit trail is not tamper-evident, and the Administrator is unchecked
threats.description: SEC-LOG-4 makes audit entries append-only from the application's perspective — but the Administrator holds every product authority, and no separation of duties, dual control or independent retention is specified anywhere. Application-level append-only does not constrain an actor with database or infrastructure access, and NFR-9.6 makes the Administrator the sole reader of the trail that would record their own actions.
threats.attackScenario: An Administrator alters a member's scores ahead of a promotion decision. The audit entries naming them are removed at the storage layer, or simply never reviewed, because the only party entitled to read the trail is the party who acted.
threats.businessImpact: Undetectable manipulation of employment-relevant records by the most privileged role, with no independent check. The audit control that the whole integrity story rests on does not cover its most capable adversary.
mitigations: Ship audit and security events to an independent, append-only sink outside the Administrator's product authority, with its own retention.
Make entries tamper-evident — hash-chain or sign them — so removal or alteration is detectable rather than merely forbidden.
Introduce separation of duties for the highest-impact operations: personal-data deletion (FR-8.4) and role assignment (FR-1.3) reviewed by a second Administrator.
Decide who reviews the audit trail. A trail nobody reads is a control in name only.
Record this as a requirement in REQUIREMENTS.md if accepted — NFR-9.6 as written does not reach it.
threats.residualRisk: medium — insider risk at the top privilege level is reduced, not removed

threats.name: Personal data, tokens or answer keys written to logs
threats.description: SEC-LOG-3 forbids credentials, session tokens, answer keys and individual score values in logs, and requires identifiers rather than personal content. The usual breach is incidental: a request-body dump on error, a verbose framework default, or an exception message carrying the payload — all of which arrive with the framework, which is TO BE DECIDED.
threats.attackScenario: An exam submission fails validation and the handler logs the full request body, placing answer selections and, from an adjacent path, answer keys into a log store with far broader access than the database.
threats.businessImpact: Sensitive data escapes the access controls built around it into a system designed for wide operational read access.
mitigations: Log identifiers and outcomes, never payloads; put redaction in the shared logging adapter rather than at each call site.
Disable framework request-body logging explicitly once the framework is chosen.
Run the log-scrubbing test SEC-LOG-3 names across authentication, exam and scoring paths.
Apply the same rule to error responses: no stack trace, query text or internal identifier reaches a caller (SEC-ERR-1).
Note that .claude/logs/tool-audit.jsonl already applies this pattern in the development tooling and is git-ignored — carry that discipline into the product.

threats.name: Formula and content injection through delimited import and export
threats.description: FR-8.2 ingests delimited files and FR-8.3 emits a machine-readable export. SEC-INPUT-5 covers the ingest side — size and type limits, no formula or external-reference evaluation, no caller-controlled storage path — but the export side is the mirror hazard: a member name stored innocently becomes an executable formula when the export is opened in a spreadsheet.
threats.attackScenario: A member's name is set to a leading-equals formula. An Administrator exports the roster and opens it; the spreadsheet executes the formula, which exfiltrates cell contents or launches a command. Alternatively an import row carries a path-traversal filename for an attached asset.
threats.businessImpact: Code execution on an Administrator's workstation from data the system itself distributed, and a route around every server-side control.

existingControls.status: Specified — limits TO BE DECIDED; export side not covered

mitigations: Neutralize leading formula characters on every exported delimited field, or export a format that does not evaluate — SEC-INPUT-5 should be extended to say so, since it currently addresses ingest only.
Enforce declared size and type limits before parsing; never store under a caller-controlled path or filename (SEC-INPUT-5).
Parse without evaluating formulas, macros or external references.
Validate each row through the owning component's rules, as SEC-INPUT-4 already requires.

threats.name: Deletion leaves residue, and deletion versus audit is unresolved
threats.description: FR-8.4 requires a deleted member and their scores to disappear from every chart, list, ranked view, export and search result. SEC-DATA-3 adds cached and derived views. Against that, NFR-9.6 and SEC-LOG-4 make audit entries naming that member append-only. SQ-6 records the conflict; nothing resolves it, and ARCHITECTURE.md independently defers the same decision.
threats.attackScenario: After a deletion, the member still appears in a cached chart dataset, a saved team, a ranked list, an export generated earlier, or an audit entry readable by an Administrator. The deletion is reported complete but is not.
threats.businessImpact: A data-subject request is answered incorrectly. If SQ-1 resolves toward GDPR, that is a compliance failure as well as a trust failure.
mitigations: Answer SQ-6 and record the decision in REQUIREMENTS.md: irreversible anonymization of the audit entry's subject reference while retaining the actor, action and timestamp is the usual reconciliation, and it satisfies both obligations.

Enumerate every surface that can return member data — charts, saved teams, ranked lists, exports, caches, derived read models, search indexes, backups — and make deletion sweep all of them (SEC-DATA-3).
Define what happens to a saved team (FR-2.4) that loses a member.
Post-deletion verification sweep as a standing test, which SEC-DATA-3 already specifies.

threats.name: Retention undefined because regulatory scope is contradictory
threats.description: REQUIREMENTS.md states no regulated data is stored; the security notes invoke GDPR and CCPA. SECURITY.md records the conflict as SQ-1 and correctly refuses to resolve it. Downstream, SEC-DATA-6 cannot state a retention period for score history, exam attempts, audit entries or authentication logs, and marks itself not verifiable. Indefinite retention of employment-relevant performance data is the default the system will ship with.
threats.attackScenario: No attack. Years of per-skill score history accumulate about every individual, available to every Administrator and to anyone who breaches any of the other findings here. The blast radius of every disclosure threat in this model grows with time, without limit.
threats.businessImpact: Unbounded breach impact, an unanswerable data-subject access request, and — if GDPR applies — a storage-limitation failure and an unidentified lawful basis.
mitigations: Answer SQ-1 first: jurisdiction, establishment, data-subject residency, controller or processor. It gates SEC-DATA-6, the rights the system must serve beyond FR-8.3 and FR-8.4, and breach-notification duties.
Set and enforce retention periods per data class even if no regime applies — a defensible default beats an accidental forever.
Resolve the contradiction in REQUIREMENTS.md, which owns the privacy-constraint statement, rather than leaving the two documents disagreeing.
Answer SQ-12 in the same pass: an incident-response path with named notification parties and timeframes.

threats.name: Server-side request forgery through dereferenced URLs
threats.description: SEC-EXT-4 forbids the server fetching a URL derived from user or imported data. The candidate sinks are asset references, import rows that might carry a media URL, and OIDC metadata discovery. Cloud metadata endpoints are the usual target and SQ-8 leaves the provider unknown, so no provider-specific hardening is specified.
threats.attackScenario: An import row supplies a media URL pointing at the cloud instance metadata service. The server fetches it and stores or returns the response, disclosing infrastructure credentials that bypass every application control.
threats.businessImpact: Infrastructure credential disclosure, escalating to full environment compromise.
mitigations: Do not dereference caller-supplied URLs at all; require assets be uploaded rather than referenced.
If a fetch is unavoidable, restrict to configured destinations by allow-list, resolve and pin the address, and deny link-local, loopback and private ranges (SEC-EXT-4).
Enforce metadata-service hardening at the infrastructure layer once SQ-8 is answered.
Treat every external response as untrusted input and fail closed (SEC-EXT-2).

threats.name: Supply chain compromise through the npm and Terraform dependency trees
threats.description: Node, React and React Native pull large transitive trees, and the single most security-relevant choice — the radar chart rendering library — is TO BE DECIDED and sits on the XSS path in T-12. DEP-1..DEP-8 are a genuinely strong written policy, but no lockfile, scanner or CI exists to apply them, and no dependency has been assessed.
threats.attackScenario: A transitive package is compromised and published. It executes during build, exfiltrating the signing key or injecting code into the client bundle that both clients distribute.
threats.businessImpact: Code execution in the build, on the server, or in every user's browser — a compromise no application-layer control in this model constrains.

existingControls.status: Written policy; nothing to apply it to

mitigations: Commit a lockfile and use frozen resolution in CI and production from the first workspace (DEP-7); npm ci is already the documented install command.
Add vulnerability scanning and a dependency-review gate in the same PR that adds the first package.json (SEC-CICD-6).
Apply DEP-2's justification requirement in PR descriptions from the first dependency, and DEP-6's transitive-tree review to the chart library in particular.
Pin build tooling and make artifacts traceable to the reviewed commit and lockfile (SEC-CICD-5).
Disable install scripts by default where the ecosystem allows.
threats.residualRisk: medium — supply chain risk is managed, never eliminated

threats.name: Secrets exposed in source, client bundles or Terraform state
threats.description: SEC-SECRET-1 through SEC-SECRET-3 cover this well, and the .claude hooks already block tool-driven writes to credential- and state-shaped paths. Two gaps remain: the .gitignore does not cover *.tfstate, *.tfstate.* or .terraform/, and a developer working outside Claude Code is not covered by the hook at all. Terraform state routinely contains secrets in plaintext.
threats.attackScenario: The first infrastructure PR commits a local state file containing database credentials and the mail provider's API key. The repository history retains them permanently, and rotation is the only remedy.
threats.businessImpact: Credential disclosure with a long tail: git history keeps the secret after the file is deleted.

existingControls.status: Specified — no CI secret scanning exists

mitigations: Add *.tfstate, *.tfstate.*, .terraform/ and *.tfvars to .gitignore now, before any Terraform file exists. This is a one-line change with a permanent payoff.
Configure a remote Terraform state backend with access control, versioning and encryption as part of SQ-8 (SEC-CICD-4).
Add secret scanning to CI over source, bundles and IaC, and a pre-commit hook so protection does not depend on which tool the developer used (SEC-SECRET-1).
Hold the JWT signing key in the secret store, rotatable without redeploy (SEC-SECRET-2), and keep only publicly disclosable configuration in client bundles (SEC-SECRET-3).

threats.name: Personal or sensitive content in outbound email
threats.description: Email is the one product data path that leaves the trust boundary into an untrusted transport and a third-party provider. SEC-EXT-3 permits only the minimum content and forbids scores, exam answers and credentials in the body. The temptation is to include a score in a result notification.
threats.attackScenario: A result email includes the member's score. Mail is retained by the provider, forwarded, and readable by anyone with mailbox access — an exposure outside every control in this model.
threats.businessImpact: Personal performance data disclosed to a third-party processor and to mailbox holders, with retention the system does not govern.
mitigations: Notify that something happened and link to the application; never carry the value itself (SEC-EXT-3).
Review every template against a permitted-field list before it ships.
Include the mail provider in the SQ-1 processor analysis; it will hold personal data regardless of body content.

threats.name: Real personal data reaches test fixtures and non-production environments
threats.description: UT-10.1 requires ten fake users with ten skill levels, used at every build step; SEC-DATA-5 requires them to be synthetic and forbids copying personal performance data into non-production environments. The pressure to seed a realistic fixture from production data is the standard cause of this failing, and CLAUDE.md makes this fixture a constant companion to every build step.
threats.attackScenario: A developer seeds the demo environment from a production export for realism. Personal performance data now sits in an environment with weaker controls and broader access.
threats.businessImpact: Personal data in an environment never designed to hold it; a breach there is a breach of the real dataset.
mitigations: Generate the UT-10.1 fixture deterministically from a seed, committed as a generator rather than as data (SEC-DATA-5).
Add a CI check asserting seed data is generated, not imported — SEC-DATA-5 already names it.
Keep the fixture usable by every build step as CLAUDE.md requires, which is easier with a generator than with a copied snapshot.

threats.name: Development-boundary weaknesses in the enforcement layer
threats.description: The .claude enforcement layer is unusually good for a project of this stage, and it is honest about its own gaps — CLAUDE.md lists what is not mechanically enforced and why. Two consequences are worth recording. First, run-tests.sh is a placeholder, so the 'tests pass before merge' rule and the 'never commit to main' rule hold by convention only. Second, this layer configures an LLM coding agent whose instructions are read from the specification documents at runtime, which makes those documents an instruction channel: a change to SECURITY.md changes agent behaviour without changing any code.
threats.attackScenario: A PR edits SECURITY.md to weaken a rule the agents read at runtime, and the enforcement layer enforces the weakened rule thereafter. Or a change lands on main with no test gate because no gate exists.
threats.businessImpact: Erosion of the project's own controls through ordinary-looking documentation changes, at a stage when the documents are the only thing that exists.
mitigations: Enable run-tests.sh with the first workspace and move the full gate into CI when the CI system is chosen (SQ-8) — CLAUDE.md already commits to this.
Treat SECURITY.md, ARCHITECTURE.md and .claude/ as security-relevant paths requiring the human security review CLAUDE.md already mandates for trust-boundary changes.
Add the PreToolUse commit hook CLAUDE.md describes but has not built, covering the never-commit-to-main and DESIGN.md/style-guide.html pairing rules.
Keep this threat out of the product trust boundary set: it is a development risk, not a runtime one.

coverageGaps.name: Single-perspective assessment throughout
coverageGaps.detail: Every finding in this model comes from one perspective: automated analysis of documents and repository contents. No human participated in any session — no security engineer, developer, privacy officer, business stakeholder or operations role. Under the pipeline's own cross-functional standard, every threat here is a single-perspective finding.

coverageGaps.name: Privacy findings lack privacy-domain review
coverageGaps.detail: T-04, T-25 and T-26 turn on regulatory scope (SQ-1) and on an unmade product decision about peer visibility (OQ-1). Neither can be settled by analysis.

coverageGaps.name: Business impact ratings lack business input
coverageGaps.detail: Impact statements here are inferred from the employment context of the data. No business stakeholder has rated what a peer score exposure or a manipulated ranking actually costs this organization.

coverageGaps.name: Infrastructure threats assessed without an infrastructure decision
coverageGaps.detail: T-13, T-27 and T-29 are provider-agnostic because SQ-8 is unanswered. Provider-specific threats cannot be enumerated until it is.

coverageGaps.name: No component-level design to review
coverageGaps.detail: Threats are enumerated against specified components, not implemented ones. Every finding must be revisited against the first implementation of the component it names.

coverageGaps.name: No abuse-case or red-team perspective
coverageGaps.detail: Attack trees (prompt 03) were not run. The exam-integrity and insider-manipulation objectives (T-15, T-22) would benefit most from that treatment.

coverageGaps.name: No reliability or FMEA perspective
coverageGaps.detail: Availability is represented by a single threat (T-19). NFR-9.1 and NFR-9.3 imply failure modes at scale that FMEA (prompt 04) would enumerate properly.

disagreements.name: Is regulated personal data in scope?
positions: REQUIREMENTS.md: no special-category or regulated data is stored
Security notes: the education context is protected by GDPR and CCPA
disagreements.resolutionOwner: Privacy officer or legal counsel with the product owner
disagreements.note: A document-level disagreement, not a session one — no human session has been held. It must be resolved before retention, deletion semantics and breach duties can be specified.

disagreements.name: May peers see each other's attributed scores?
positions: FR-1.4: a Team Member must not view another individual's scores
FR-7.3 and FR-6.2: chart series are attributed by name and available as a table from one dataset
disagreements.resolutionOwner: Product owner with HR or people operations

disagreements.name: Should self-assessed scores drive the chart?
positions: FR-5.2 and FR-4.6 read together: yes, the most recent score is current
OQ-3: unanswered, implying the authors were not settled

assumptions: No implementation exists; every control is Specified — Not Implemented and no finding asserts a running vulnerability.
Severity rates design-stage risk carried into implementation, per the scoring convention in metadata.
The four roles, most privacy constraints and many requirements are marked (assumed) at source in REQUIREMENTS.md; the authorization model rests on them.
Exam media exists, per an ARCHITECTURE.md ASSUMPTION. If exams carry no media, T-09 and boundary tb-3 leave scope.
No AI/ML component exists in the product; MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP ML Top 10 are out of scope. The only AI surface is the development tooling (T-32).
Enterprise scale is taken as NFR-9.3: 1,000 team members, 100 skills.
The security notes referenced by SECURITY.md are not in the repository; their content is known only through SECURITY.md's restatement.
This model supersedes nothing: SECURITY.md records its threat model status as TO BE COMPLETED, so there is no prior baseline to diff.
